items.title: The two-point duplication property of a function family relative to a target function
Unital point-separating real vector sublattices of $C(X,\mathbb R)$
Unital, point-separating, and nowhere-vanishing real function algebras on a compact Hausdorff space
Self-adjoint complex function algebras, unitality, and point separation
The general real function-algebra definition agrees with the published compact-metric definition
items.strategy: Give the metric space its metric topology. Use the published equivalence between metric and topological compactness, metric Hausdorff separation, and the metric/topological continuity equivalence to identify both ambient spaces of continuous functions. Then compare the algebra, constant, and point-separation clauses one by one. No assertion is made for the empty metric space, which the earlier definition excludes.

items.title: A unital separating real function lattice interpolates arbitrary values at two distinct points
items.strategy: For distinct $x,y$, choose a separator $g$ and apply an affine rescaling so that its values at $x,y$ are the prescribed pair; vector-space and constant closure keep the rescaling in the lattice. When the later sweep encounters $x=y$, use the corresponding constant function rather than invoking this distinct-point lemma.

items.title: A function lattice with the two-point duplication property uniformly approximates its target
items.strategy: Let a sublattice $L\subseteq C(X,\mathbb R)$ have the two-point duplication property relative to $f$. For each $x$, duplicate $f$ at $x$ and every $y$; continuity gives neighbourhoods on which the witnesses lie below $f+\varepsilon$. Compactness leaves finitely many, and their pointwise maximum gives $g_x$ with $g_x>f-\varepsilon$ near $x$ and $g_x<f+\varepsilon$ everywhere. A second finite cover and pointwise minimum gives one member of $L$ within $\varepsilon$ of $f$ everywhere. Define both covering families by their properties and make only the resulting finite choices.

items.title: Lattice Stone–Weierstrass theorem on a compact Hausdorff space
items.strategy: For every target $f\in C(X,\mathbb R)$, the interpolation lemma gives the vector sublattice the two-point duplication property relative to $f$. Apply the general two-sweep lemma at every positive error. This is uniform density. Handle the empty compact space directly, since it has a unique real-valued function, before invoking the nonempty-domain uniform-topology definition.

items.title: The uniform closure of a real function algebra is a vector lattice
items.strategy: First verify that uniform limits preserve the algebra operations. For $f$ in the closure, compactness bounds its image in $[-M,M]$. Approximate $|t|$ there by polynomials, subtract each polynomial's constant term when the algebra is nonunital, and use the available unit when it is unital, to place $|f|$ in the closure. Then use $f\vee g=(f+g+|f-g|)/2$ and $f\wedge g=(f+g-|f-g|)/2$. Treat $M=0$ separately.

items.title: Real Stone–Weierstrass theorem for compact Hausdorff spaces
items.strategy: The uniform closure of the unital separating algebra remains unital and separating and is a real vector lattice by the closure lemma. Apply lattice Stone–Weierstrass to that closure; being both dense and closed, it is all of $C(X,\mathbb R)$. Include the empty-space boundary directly.

items.title: A nowhere-vanishing real function algebra on a compact space approximates the constant one
items.strategy: For every point choose an algebra member nonzero there. Compactness reduces the corresponding nonzero neighbourhoods to finitely many, and the sum of their squares is an algebra member $h$ with positive minimum $m$ and finite maximum $M$. Approximate $1/t$ on $[m,M]$ by a polynomial $p$; then $hp(h)$ lies in the possibly nonunital algebra and uniformly approximates one. Handle the empty domain and the one-point range $m=M$ explicitly.

items.title: A separating real function algebra is dense or its closure consists exactly of the functions vanishing at one point
items.strategy: Let $B$ be the uniform closure. If the algebra has no common zero, the preceding approximate-unit lemma puts the constant one in $B$, and real Stone–Weierstrass gives $B=C(X,\mathbb R)$. If all algebra members vanish at $x_0$, separation makes $x_0$ unique. The algebra obtained by adjoining constants is unital and separating, hence dense; evaluating an approximant $a+c$ at $x_0$ shows that every continuous function vanishing at $x_0$ is approximated by members $a$ of the original algebra. Thus $B$ is exactly that vanishing ideal. Handle the empty space separately.

items.title: A point-separating nowhere-vanishing real function algebra is uniformly dense
items.strategy: Apply the separating-algebra dichotomy. Its proper alternative requires every algebra member to vanish at one fixed point, contradicting nowhere-vanishing there. Hence the closure is all of $C(X,\mathbb R)$.

items.title: The real-valued part of a self-adjoint complex function algebra is separating and has the same common zeros
items.strategy: Self-adjointness puts $(f+\overline f)/2$ and $(f-\overline f)/(2i)$ in the algebra, so the real and imaginary parts of every member lie in its real-valued part. If $f$ separates two points, at least one of those two parts separates them. Verify real-scalar, sum, and product closure pointwise using the published complex field and conjugation laws.

items.title: Complex Stone–Weierstrass dichotomy for separating self-adjoint algebras; the unital case is dense
items.strategy: Apply the real separating-algebra dichotomy to the real-valued part of the self-adjoint algebra. In the dense alternative, approximate the real and imaginary parts of an arbitrary continuous complex function separately and combine them as $u+iv$. In the proper alternative, the same argument identifies the complex closure with all continuous functions vanishing at the unique common zero. A unital algebra has no common zero, so the named unital self-adjoint form is dense. Self-adjointness is indispensable and is not inferred from point separation.

items.title: The unital algebra generated by a separating complex family and its conjugates is dense
items.strategy: The generated algebra contains constants, retains the original separating family, and is closed under conjugation because the generators occur in conjugate pairs and complex conjugation respects pointwise sums and products. Apply complex Stone–Weierstrass.

items.title: The quotient that identifies points indistinguishable by a real function algebra
A closed unital real function algebra is $C(Y,\mathbb R)$ on its indistinguishability quotient
items.strategy: Let $q:X\to Y$ be the quotient by equality of all algebra values. Each algebra member descends uniquely and continuously; the descended algebra separates points. The quotient is compact as a continuous image and Hausdorff because a descended real function separates any two distinct classes. Real Stone–Weierstrass makes the descended algebra dense in $C(Y,\mathbb R)$; pulling uniform approximations back along surjective $q$ and using closedness upgrades density to equality and yields an isometric algebra isomorphism.

title: Stone–Weierstrass in General: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The disc algebra is unital and separating but not self-adjoint or dense
items.strategy: On the closed unit disc let $A$ be the uniform closure of polynomials in the coordinate $z$. The published complex metric identifies the disc with a closed bounded subset of Euclidean $\mathbb R^2$; Heine–Borel and the metric/topological compactness bridge make it compact Hausdorff. If $\overline z\in A$, choose a polynomial $p$ uniformly closer than one to it and set $N=\deg p+2$. De Moivre writes all $N$th roots as powers of $\zeta=\exp(2\pi i/N)$, while the exponential-kernel theorem proves $\zeta^r\ne1$ for $1\le r<N$. Prove $(x-1)\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}x^k=x^N-1$ inline by induction and use it to obtain every shifted-power cancellation not already supplied by the exact root-sum corollary. Averaging $\zeta^k p(\zeta^k)$ then gives zero, while averaging $\zeta^k\overline{\zeta^k}$ gives one, contradicting the uniform error. Hence $A$ is not self-adjoint and, being closed and proper, is not dense.

items.title: Trigonometric polynomials are uniformly dense on the unit circle
items.strategy: Define complex trigonometric polynomials as finite Laurent sums $\sum_{j=-n}^n a_jz^j$, using the published integer-power convention. On the unit circle, $z\overline z=|z|^2=1$, so a numbered algebra step proves $z^{-1}=\overline z$ and converts negative powers into powers of the conjugate coordinate. The published complex metric makes the circle a closed bounded Euclidean subset; Heine–Borel and the metric/topological bridges make it compact Hausdorff. Constants, the coordinate separator, and conjugation closure then satisfy complex Stone–Weierstrass; no Fourier convergence theorem is used.

items.title: The lattice generated by distance functions is dense on every compact metric space
items.strategy: Let $L$ be the smallest real vector sublattice containing constants and all functions $d(a,-)$. Every distance function is continuous by the triangle inequality, and for $x\ne y$ the function $d(x,-)$ takes the distinct values $0$ and $d(x,y)$. Thus $L$ separates points and lattice Stone–Weierstrass applies.

items.title: On a finite compact Hausdorff space a unital separating algebra contains every scalar-valued function
items.strategy: For each point $x$ and every other point $y$, normalize a separator to equal one at $x$ and zero at $y$. Their finite product is the indicator of $x$. Linear combinations of these indicators reproduce every real- or complex-valued function exactly. Treat the empty and one-point spaces separately; on a finite Hausdorff space every scalar-valued function is continuous.

items.title: Endpoint-duplicating functions on $[0,1]$ become all continuous functions on the endpoint quotient
items.strategy: Take the real algebra of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ satisfying $f(0)=f(1)$. It is closed and unital. Explicit piecewise-linear tent functions with equal endpoint values separate every pair except the endpoint pair, so its indistinguishability quotient identifies exactly $0$ and $1$. The quotient representation theorem identifies the algebra isometrically with all continuous real functions on that quotient.

items.title: The polynomial algebra is dense but not closed on a nondegenerate compact interval
items.strategy: For $a<b$, polynomials restricted to $[a,b]$ form a unital separating algebra, so Stone–Weierstrass gives density. Choose $c$ strictly between the endpoints; the continuous function $|x-c|$ cannot agree with a polynomial because its one-sided slopes at $c$ differ. Hence the algebra is proper, and a proper dense subspace is not closed.
